matches.rationale: GT1 concerns overstating a 'clear linear relationship' and saturation claims in the Abstract that are not fully supported by later results. Pred_id 1 discusses understatement of correlation strength (moderate vs. moderate-to-strong), which is the opposite issue and does not address the overstatement of saturation or linear relationship claims.

GT2 identifies a fabricated citation 'Grant, 2025' and overly specific claims about whiskers in hunting/low-light environments in the Introduction. None of the findings mention fabricated references or this specific biological claim.
GT3 concerns the inconsistency of a 5×7 array with zero padding for 30 whiskers in the Method section. None of the findings address this specific whisker array configuration issue.

GT4 identifies missing hyperparameter adjustments and training protocol details to balance learning across two different datasets. None of the findings discuss this specific protocol fairness issue regarding the two whisking datasets.

GT5 concerns selective reporting that inflates effectiveness by emphasizing only top models saturating variance. Pred_id 10 directly addresses this, noting the claim of 'saturated all explainable neural variance' and 'robustly passing' tests overstates findings given limited stimulus diversity (only 6 stimuli).

GT6 concerns overgeneralization about tactile augmentations being critical and image augmentations causing training failure. None of the findings discuss this specific augmentation comparison rhetoric.

GT7 identifies an ethical omission regarding insufficient reflection on data scarcity limiting generalizability. While pred_id 10 mentions limited stimulus diversity, it focuses on overstated claims rather than ethical transparency about dataset constraints.

GT8 concerns the ±1 N force clipping range being potentially unrealistic (one tenth of maximal bite force) without justification. None of the findings address this specific force simulation parameter issue.
GT9 identifies missing detailed hyperparameter reporting for SSL vs. supervised training stages. None of the findings discuss this specific computational budget or hyperparameter documentation issue.

GT10 concerns Table 6 reporting zero accuracies for several models where chance is 0.5 or 0.33, suggesting errors or missing data. Pred_id 9 identifies exactly this issue in Table 6, noting suspiciously low (at-chance) performance for specific models.
GT11 concerns equation numbering skips and undefined variables (y_t^ℓ) in the IntersectionRNN Appendix equations. None of the findings discuss these specific mathematical notation issues.

GT12 identifies cross-section inconsistency where the Abstract claims saturation of explainable variance but Discussion acknowledges limited dataset diversity. Pred_id 10 captures this by noting the saturation claim overstates generalizability given the acknowledged 'critical limitation' of limited stimulus diversity.

GT13 concerns speculative overextension in the Discussion suggesting GPT-based attenders imply biological attention mechanisms. None of the findings address this specific interpretability claim about attention mechanisms.
GT14 identifies failure to discuss biases from small sample size (11 mice, 999 units). None of the findings explicitly address this ethical reporting omission regarding sample size limitations.

GT15 concerns unfair comparisons between ConvRNN and other architectures due to unbalanced parameter counts or compute budgets. None of the findings discuss this specific experimental design fairness issue.

GT16 identifies neural fit scores exceeding the maximum inter-animal consistency (1.34 reported in Fig. 4b), suggesting overfitting or calculation errors. Pred_id 4 directly identifies the impossible maximum of 1.34 for correlation metrics, and pred_id 5 notes models appearing to exceed the stated maximum of 0.34, both capturing this data integrity issue.

GT17 concerns fabricated claims in Related Work about being the first neural comparison across 64 models, misrepresenting cited works on visual (not tactile) cortex. None of the findings address this specific citation misrepresentation or novelty fabrication.
